Leaven is any substance that makes dough rise — that is, any ingredient you add to a mixture of flour and water (dough or batter) that causes it to puff up, become lighter, and grow in volume before or during baking.

Think of the difference between a flat, dense cracker and a soft, airy loaf of bread. The thing responsible for that transformation — for making the dough "wake up" and rise — is the leaven.

Leaven works by producing gas (mainly carbon dioxide) inside the dough. This gas gets trapped in the dough as tiny bubbles, which expand and push the dough outward and upward, making it light and airy. When the dough is baked, those air pockets set permanently, giving bread its soft, spongy texture.

The crucial thing to understand is the sheer power of proportion: a very small amount of leaven is enough to transform a large amount of dough. You don't need much — a little goes a long way. This proportion is central to the word's deeper meaning (more on that below).

Leaven is not one specific ingredient — it's a category. Anything that causes dough to rise qualifies. The most common examples are:

Yeast — the oldest and most traditional leaven. It is a living microorganism. When mixed into dough, it eats the sugars present and releases carbon dioxide gas as a by-product, causing the dough to rise slowly over hours. This is how classic bread, pizza dough, and brioche are made.

Sourdough starter — a naturally fermented mixture of flour and water that contains wild yeast and bacteria. It works the same way as commercial yeast but more slowly, and it gives bread a tangy, complex flavour. Many traditional cultures around the world developed this form of leaven long before commercial yeast existed.

Baking powder and baking soda — chemical leavens. Unlike yeast, they are not living organisms and they work much faster — almost instantly when exposed to moisture and/or heat. They are used in cakes, muffins, pancakes, and quick breads where you don't want to wait hours for the dough to rise.

All of these are "leaven" in the noun sense — they are the rising agent.
The figurative meaning — and why it matters

Because of its physical behaviour (a tiny amount quietly spreading through and transforming a much larger whole), "leaven" developed a powerful metaphorical meaning in general language.

In its figurative sense, leaven refers to any influence, idea, quality, or element that, when introduced into a larger group or situation, gradually spreads and changes the nature of the whole. It is something that works quietly from within, not by force from outside.

For example:

  • "Her optimism was a leaven in the otherwise discouraged team." — Her positive attitude, though just one person's quality, spread through and lifted the entire group.
  • "The arrival of a few experienced teachers acted as a leaven in the school." — A small number of skilled people transformed the entire institution.

Notice that the figurative use preserves the same logic as the literal use: small quantity, large and thorough transformation, working from the inside out. The word carries that sense of quiet, pervasive power whenever it is used metaphorically.

The figurative meaning can be positive or negative. Leaven can represent a positive transforming force (hope, wisdom, energy lifting a whole group), or it can represent a corrupting influence that spreads and contaminates (a single bad attitude infecting an entire organisation). Context determines which is meant.

The word carries enormous cultural and religious weight, particularly in Jewish and Christian traditions, and you will encounter it frequently in literature, speeches, and religious texts — so understanding this context is essential.

In Judaism, leaven holds deep ritual significance. During the festival of Passover (Pesach), all leavened food — anything containing leaven or made with it — must be removed from the home and must not be eaten for seven days. This is in memory of the Israelites' hasty departure from Egypt, when they had no time to let their bread rise, so they ate flat, unleavened bread (matzo). The search for and removal of leaven before Passover is a meaningful and serious religious ritual. The Hebrew word for leavened food is chametz, and avoiding it is a biblical commandment. In this tradition, leaven can symbolise pride and corruption — things that "puff up."

In Christianity, Jesus uses leaven in two very different ways in the New Testament, which illustrates how the word can cut both ways:

  • In a positive sense, Jesus compares the Kingdom of Heaven to leaven that a woman mixes into a large batch of flour — it spreads quietly and invisibly through the whole, transforming everything. This presents leaven as a picture of unstoppable, pervasive goodness.
  • In a negative sense, Jesus warns his disciples to beware of "the leaven of the Pharisees" — meaning their hypocrisy and false teaching, which, like yeast in dough, would spread and corrupt thinking if left unchecked.

These two uses perfectly capture the dual nature of the figurative meaning: transforming power that can go either way, depending on what the leaven is.
A summary of the noun in one sentence

Leaven is any substance that causes dough to rise by producing gas within it — classically yeast — and, by extension in figurative use, any small but powerful influence that quietly spreads through and transforms something much larger than itself, for better or worse.
